intro: Six matriculation-exam-style problems bring together the lesson's energy, power and efficiency. Solve them as in the exam: justify the choice of model, solve for the quantity asked before substituting the numbers and assess whether the result is reasonable. Open the model answer and the scoring guide only when your solution is ready.

tasks.title: Solar power at the cottage
tasks.source_note: The cottage, the devices and the production figures are invented examples that match the order of magnitude of an ordinary small solar power system.
tasks.text:
A summer cottage on an island has no connection to the power grid. On the roof are solar panels with a rated power of $1.2\,\text{kW}$. The electricity from the panels is stored in a battery, and an inverter converts the battery's electricity into a form suitable for the devices. The combined efficiency of charging and discharging the battery is $90\,\%$ and that of the inverter $93\,\%$.

The cottage's electrical devices on an ordinary summer day:

| Device | Power | Use per day |
|---|---|---|
| fridge | $45\,\text{W}$ | $24\,\text{h}$ |
| LED lamps | $6 \cdot 7.0\,\text{W}$ | $5.0\,\text{h}$ |
| coffee maker | $1.0\,\text{kW}$ | $15\,\text{min}$ |

The power of the fridge is an average power, because its compressor runs only part of the time.

The panels' display shows that on a sunny day the panels produced $5.4\,\text{kWh}$ and on a cloudy day $1.5\,\text{kWh}$.

parts.text: How much electrical energy do the cottage's devices use in a day?

criteria.detail: The energy of each device is $E = P\,t$, and the energies are added up.
Fridge $1.08\,\text{kWh}$, lamps $0.21\,\text{kWh}$ and coffee maker $0.25\,\text{kWh}$; minutes converted to hours.
$1.5\,\text{kWh}$ (about $5.5\,\text{MJ}$) to two significant figures.

parts.text: How much electricity must the panels produce in a day so that the need in part a is covered through the battery and the inverter? Is the production of a cloudy day enough?

criteria.text: Justifies that the battery and the inverter are in series, so their efficiencies are multiplied.

criteria.detail: $E_\text{panels} = \dfrac{E_\text{need}}{\eta_\text{batt}\,\eta_\text{inv}}$
$E_\text{panels} \approx 1.8\,\text{kWh}$
The $1.5\,\text{kWh}$ of a cloudy day is not enough: only about $1.3\,\text{kWh}$ of it reaches the devices, so the battery runs down unless the surplus of a sunny day is in storage.

parts.text: The cottage's neighbour says: “The panels' power is $1.2\,\text{kW}$, so they produce $1.2\,\text{kWh}$ a day.” Evaluate the claim.

criteria.text: Tells power and energy apart: the kilowatt tells the rate of production, the kilowatt-hour the amount of energy; energy is power multiplied by time.
Uses the data: on a sunny day $5.4\,\text{kWh}$ corresponds to $4.5$ hours at rated power, on a cloudy day only about one hour.

criteria.detail: The claim is wrong: the day's energy depends on how strongly and how long the sun shines, and the rated power is the maximum power.

tasks.title: The wood chip power plant
tasks.source_note: The plant and its numbers are invented examples. The heat of combustion of forest chips, $9.5\,\text{MJ/kg}$, is typical of moist chips, and the actual value varies with the moisture content.
tasks.text:
A town's combined heat and power plant burns forest chips and produces both electricity and district heat. On a frosty day the following were read from the screen in the plant's control room:

- chips are fed into the boiler at $42\,\text{t}$ per hour
- heat of combustion of the chips $9.5\,\text{MJ/kg}$
- electrical power $30\,\text{MW}$
- district heating power $70\,\text{MW}$

For comparison, the same electricity could be produced in a condensing power plant with an efficiency of $38\,\%$, and the same district heat in a boiler producing only heat, with an efficiency of $90\,\%$.

parts.text: How large is the fuel power of the plant?

criteria.detail: $E = Hm$ for the chips burnt in an hour and $P_0 = \dfrac{E}{t}$
$E = 9.5\,\text{MJ}/\text{kg} \cdot 42\,000\,\text{kg} = 399\,000\,\text{MJ}$ and $t = 3600\,\text{s}$; the tonnes and the hour converted by substitution.
$P_0 \approx 1.1 \cdot 10^{2}\,\text{MW}$ (more precisely $110.8\,\text{MW}$)

parts.text: Calculate the electrical efficiency and the overall efficiency of the plant.

criteria.detail: $\eta_\text{el} = \dfrac{P_\text{el}}{P_0}$ and $\eta_\text{tot} = \dfrac{P_\text{el} + P_\text{dh}}{P_0}$
Both efficiencies from the fuel power of part a.
$\eta_\text{el} \approx 27\,\%$ and $\eta_\text{tot} \approx 90\,\%$

parts.text: How many tonnes of chips per hour would be needed if the same electricity and the same district heat were produced separately in a condensing power plant and a heating boiler?

criteria.text: Solves the fuel power of each plant separately from its useful power, $P_0 = P_\text{a} : \eta$, and adds them up.

criteria.detail: $78.9\,\text{MW} + 77.8\,\text{MW} \approx 157\,\text{MW}$ and the mass $m = \dfrac{P_0\,t}{H}$
about $59\,\text{t}$ per hour, that is, about $17\,\text{t}$ more than in combined heat and power

parts.text: In summer district heat is needed only for hot tap water. Explain why the overall efficiency of the plant does not then stay the same if it produces the same electrical power.

criteria.text: Explains that the heat of the condenser is useful only when there is a use for it as district heat; otherwise it must be given off to the surroundings as waste heat.

criteria.detail: The overall efficiency falls towards the electrical efficiency, so in summer the plant is run at a lower power or the electricity is produced elsewhere.

tasks.title: Frost and the electricity bill
tasks.source_note: The data are an invented example: the numbers are calculated from a model in which the other electricity consumption is about $12\,\text{kWh}$ a day and the heating increases steadily as the outdoor temperature falls, and variation like that of measurements has been added to them.
tasks.text:
A detached house is heated with direct electric heating, and the indoor temperature is kept at $21\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The electricity company's app shows the house's electricity consumption day by day. For one week in January the family recorded the daily consumption $E$ and the average outdoor temperature $T$ of the day. The electricity consumption other than heating, such as lighting, cooking and appliances, is about $12\,\text{kWh}$ a day in the house.

| Day | $T\ ({}^\circ\text{C})$ | $E\ (\text{kWh})$ |
|---|---|---|
| 7 Jan | $-4$ | $112$ |
| 8 Jan | $-10$ | $139$ |
| 9 Jan | $-16$ | $174$ |
| 10 Jan | $-19$ | $186$ |
| 11 Jan | $-13$ | $155$ |
| 12 Jan | $-7$ | $126$ |
| 13 Jan | $-1$ | $100$ |
| 14 Jan | $2$ | $83$ |

parts.text: Present the daily consumption as a function of the outdoor temperature in a graph, and fit a suitable model to the points.

criteria.detail: On the horizontal axis $T\ ({}^\circ\text{C})$ with its negative values, on the vertical axis $E\ (\text{kWh})$.
A falling straight line is fitted to the points, passing between them; the points are not joined into a broken line.

parts.text: Determine the slope of the line from the graph. By how much does the heating power increase for each kelvin the outdoor temperature falls? Answer in watts per kelvin.

criteria.detail: The slope from two points of the line far apart, for example $(-20\,{}^\circ\text{C};\ 191\,\text{kWh})$ and $(0\,{}^\circ\text{C};\ 93\,\text{kWh})$: about $-4.9\,\text{kWh}/{}^\circ\text{C}$ per day.

criteria.text: Interprets the slope: the daily heating energy increases by about $4.9\,\text{kWh}$ when the outdoor temperature falls by one kelvin.

criteria.detail: The average power is the energy divided by the time: $P = \dfrac{E}{t}$, $t = 24\,\text{h}$.
$4.9\,\text{kWh} : 24\,\text{h} \approx 0.20\,\text{kW}$, that is, about $200\,\text{W}$ per kelvin; a result of $192$–$216\,\text{W/K}$ is accepted.

parts.text: Use the graph to estimate the house's electricity consumption on a day whose average temperature is $-28\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. Assess how reliable the estimate is.

criteria.detail: The line has been extended outside the measured range, or the equation of the line $E = kT + b$ has been used.
$E \approx 93\,\text{kWh} + 4.9\,\text{kWh}/{}^\circ\text{C} \cdot 28\,{}^\circ\text{C} \approx 230\,\text{kWh}$

The estimate is an extrapolation $9\,\text{K}$ outside the measured range, so it holds only if the model stays a straight line; a strong wind or the maximum power of the heaters can change the result.

parts.text: At what outdoor temperature would the house, according to the model, need no heating at all? Explain why this temperature is not the same as the indoor temperature $21\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.

criteria.detail: The temperature at which $E = 12\,\text{kWh}$ is read from the line: about $16$–$17\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.

criteria.text: Explains with conservation of energy: the electrical energy of the appliances, the heat of the people and solar radiation become heat indoors, so they make up for part of the heat losses.

criteria.detail: Heating is needed only when the outdoor temperature is below about $17\,{}^\circ\text{C}$; the accuracy of the model is limited by, for example, the sun and the wind, which the data do not separate.

tasks.title: The island's electricity
tasks.source_note: The island, the options and their numbers are invented examples. The emission factor of diesel is a rounded order-of-magnitude value.
tasks.text:
An island in an archipelago municipality has $400$ inhabitants. Its electricity is now produced in a diesel power plant. The island's electricity consumption is $3.0\,\text{GWh}$ a year, and the winter consumption peak is $1.2\,\text{MW}$. The municipality is comparing three options.

| Option | Power |
|---|---|
| A: diesel power plant (current) | $1.5\,\text{MW}$ |
| B: wind turbines and a battery | $2 \cdot 1.0\,\text{MW}$ |
| C: submarine cable to the mainland | $5\,\text{MW}$ |

- A: emission factor about $700\,\text{g/kWh}$, the fuel is brought by ship.
- B: the average power of the wind turbines is about $30\,\%$ of the rated power, and the battery holds $2.0\,\text{MWh}$.
- C: the cable is $12\,\text{km}$ long and the transmission loss is about $3\,\%$.

At the meeting of the municipal council two claims were made: “The wind turbines produce more in a year than the island consumes, so the diesel plant can be dismantled” and “Wind power is completely emission-free”.

parts.text: Evaluate the first claim. Justify your answer with a calculation.

criteria.text: Calculates the wind turbines' annual energy from the average power: $2.0\,\text{MW} \cdot 0.30 \cdot 8760\,\text{h} \approx 5.3\,\text{GWh}$, which is more than $3.0\,\text{GWh}$.
Tells energy and power apart: production must match consumption at every moment, and in calm weather the wind turbines produce nothing.
Calculates that a full battery covers the $1.2\,\text{MW}$ peak for only $2.0\,\text{MWh} : 1.2\,\text{MW} \approx 1.7\,\text{h}$.

criteria.detail: The claim does not hold: the year's energy is enough, but for calm periods dispatchable power or a connection to the grid is needed.

parts.text: Compare the options using at least three criteria and make a reasoned recommendation.

criteria.text: Uses at least three criteria of comparison, for example controllability, security of supply, emissions, transport of fuel and price.
Justifies each comparison with the properties of the options, for example the cable brings the dispatchable power of the mainland grid and its loss is small.

criteria.detail: The recommendation follows from the comparison, for example the cable and wind power together and diesel as backup power.

parts.text: Evaluate the second claim. How large are the annual carbon dioxide emissions of the diesel power plant, and how are they compared with the emissions of wind power?

criteria.text: Calculates the emissions of diesel: $m = e \cdot E = 700\,\text{g}/\text{kWh} \cdot 3.0 \cdot 10^{6}\,\text{kWh} = 2.1 \cdot 10^{9}\,\text{g} = 2100\,\text{t}$.

Explains life-cycle emissions: manufacturing, transporting and building a wind turbine cause emissions even though operating it does not, so the emissions are not zero but are much smaller than those of diesel.

criteria.detail: The claim is inaccurate: wind power is low-emission, not emission-free.

tasks.title: The efficiency of a kettle
tasks.source_note: The report and its measurement results are invented examples.
tasks.text:
A group of students wanted to check the manufacturer's claim that an electric kettle “transfers more than $90\,\%$ of the electrical energy into the water”. An extract from the group's report:

> We filled the kettle's jug to $1.0$ litre by its scale with tap water at a temperature of $15\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. We started the kettle and the timing at the same time. The kettle switched itself off when the water boiled, $3\,\text{min}\ 5\,\text{s}$ after starting. After the kettle had switched off, we opened the lid and measured the temperature of the water with a thermometer as $96\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The power on the kettle's rating plate is $2200\,\text{W}$. We calculated the efficiency as $83\,\%$, so the manufacturer's claim does not hold.

The specific heat capacity of water is $4190\,\text{J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}$, and a litre of water weighs about $1.0\,\text{kg}$.

parts.text: Show how the group got $83\,\%$ as the efficiency.

criteria.detail: $\eta = \dfrac{Q}{E}$, where $Q = cm\Delta T$ and $E = P\,t$
$Q = 4190\,\text{J}/(\text{kg} \cdot \text{K}) \cdot 1.0\,\text{kg} \cdot 81\,\text{K} \approx 339\,\text{kJ}$ and $E = 2200\,\text{W} \cdot 185\,\text{s} = 407\,\text{kJ}$
$\eta \approx 0.83 = 83\,\%$ to two significant figures

parts.text: Assess whether the group's conclusion is justified. Name the most important sources of error in the measurement and tell in which direction each changes the result.

criteria.detail: Names sources of error and tells in which direction each changes the result: for example, the temperature of the water was measured only after the kettle switched off, when the water had already cooled (makes the result smaller); the power on the rating plate is not a measured power (can change the result in either direction, because the actual power depends on the mains voltage); the amount of water was read from the jug's scale (either direction); part of the energy heated the jug (a real loss).

Assesses the size of the effect: for example, a power of $2100\,\text{W}$ would give $87\,\%$ and $1.05\,\text{kg}$ of water would give $88\,\%$, so the uncertainty of the result is several percentage points.
One measurement with such a large uncertainty is not enough to show that the claim is wrong.

parts.text: The group suspects that the efficiency depends on the amount of water. Plan an experiment that can find this out reliably.

criteria.text: Varies only the amount of water (for example $0.50$–$1.5\,\text{kg}$) and keeps the other factors constant: the same initial temperature, the same kettle, the lid closed.

Measures the necessary quantities reliably: the mass with a balance, the electrical energy with an energy meter, the temperature of stirred water before boiling, for example when the water is at $80\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.
Repeats the measurements and presents the results in a graph, for example the efficiency as a function of the amount of water, and assesses their uncertainty.

tasks.title: The pumped-storage plant in the mine
tasks.source_note: The mine and the plant's numbers are invented examples. The efficiencies are typical values for a pumped-storage plant.
tasks.text:
A pumped-storage power plant is being planned for a closed mine. The upper reservoir is at ground level, and the mine's tunnels $1.20\,\text{km}$ deeper serve as the lower reservoir. When electricity is needed, water from the upper reservoir flows down a pipe and turns a turbine and a generator at the bottom of the mine. When electricity is available cheaply, for example on a windy night, the same machines pump the water back up.

- volume of the upper reservoir $7.50 \cdot 10^{4}\,\text{m}^3$, density of water $1000\,\text{kg/m}^3$
- efficiency of the turbine and the generator $88\,\%$
- efficiency of the pump and the motor $85\,\%$
- the full upper reservoir is emptied steadily in $6.0$ hours

parts.text: How much potential energy does the water of the full upper reservoir have compared with the lower reservoir? Give the answer in megawatt-hours.

criteria.detail: $E_\text{p} = mgh$, where $m = \rho V$
$m = 7.50 \cdot 10^{7}\,\text{kg}$ and $E_\text{p} \approx 8.83 \cdot 10^{11}\,\text{J}$

criteria.text: Converts the joules to megawatt-hours by substituting $1\,\text{MWh} = 10^{6}\,\text{W} \cdot 3600\,\text{s}$.

criteria.detail: $E_\text{p} \approx 245\,\text{MWh}$ to three significant figures

parts.text: How large is the electrical power of the plant when the reservoir is emptied?

criteria.detail: $P = \dfrac{\eta_\text{t}\,E_\text{p}}{t}$
Electrical energy $0.88 \cdot 245\,\text{MWh} \approx 216\,\text{MWh}$
$P \approx 36\,\text{MW}$ to two significant figures like the time $6.0\,\text{h}$
For example, compared with the rated power of a wind turbine, the plant corresponds to about ten large wind turbines.

parts.text: How much electrical energy must be taken from the grid when the empty upper reservoir is pumped full? What is the overall efficiency of the storage when the reservoir is first filled and then emptied?

criteria.text: Justifies that pumping needs more electricity than the potential energy the water gains: $E_\text{grid} = E_\text{p} : \eta_\text{p}$.

criteria.detail: The overall efficiency is the product of the successive stages, $\eta = \eta_\text{p}\,\eta_\text{t}$.
$E_\text{grid} \approx 289\,\text{MWh}$
$\eta \approx 0.75 = 75\,\%$; check $216\,\text{MWh} : 289\,\text{MWh} \approx 0.75$

parts.text: The designer says: “The plant produces $216\,\text{MWh}$ of electricity every day.” Evaluate the claim and explain why the plant can still be useful.

criteria.text: States on the basis of conservation of energy that a pumped-storage plant does not produce energy but stores it: it takes more from the grid than it gives, about $73\,\text{MWh}$ in each filling and emptying.
Justifies the benefit: energy is shifted in time from moments of cheap overproduction to consumption peaks, and the plant is quickly controllable power alongside wind power.

criteria.detail: The claim is misleading; correctly: the plant gives $216\,\text{MWh}$ to the grid later from the $289\,\text{MWh}$ it took.
